title: An Introduction to Theoretical Mathematics
passages: Most people meet mathematics as a tool for calculating things. Pure, or THEORETICAL, mathematics is different: it studies numbers and shapes as ABSTRACT objects, purely for the sake of understanding them. A pure mathematician is far less interested in the answer to a sum than in a much deeper question: how can we be absolutely certain that something is true, everywhere and forever?

The method is RIGOROUS (strict, exact, precise). Mathematicians begin with AXIOMS, basic statements assumed to be true without proof, and then use careful DEDUCTION to build new truths from them. A statement proved this way is called A THEOREM, and once proved it is true permanently. Mathematicians usually work by observing patterns, asking why, and testing ideas. Around 300 BC, the Greek thinker EUCLID showed the power of this approach. His masterwork, the ELEMENTS, gathered 13 books containing 465 propositions, every one of them deduced from a mere handful of axioms. His methods still shape mathematics today.

A PRIME NUMBER is a whole number greater than 1 that can be divided evenly only by 1 and itself. The primes begin 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, and continue forever. They are often called THE BUILDING BLOCKS of arithmetic, because every other whole number can be made by multiplying primes together in exactly one way. Curiously, 2 is the only even prime, since every other even number is divisible by 2.

Around 2,300 years ago, EUCLID proved something remarkable: the primes are INFINITE (endless, limitless), never running out no matter how far you count. Yet primes still guard deep mysteries. In 1742, a mathematician named GOLDBACH proposed that every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes. Computers have verified this CONJECTURE for enormous numbers, but nobody has ever PROVED it. The largest prime below 100 is 97.

Here is an idea that sounds impossible: some infinities are larger than others. In 1874, the mathematician GEORG CANTOR proved it. He showed that the counting numbers form a COUNTABLE infinity, meaning you could in principle list them one by one. But the decimal numbers between 0 and 1 form an UNCOUNTABLE infinity, a set so vast it cannot be listed at all, even given forever.

Cantor's result was so PERPLEXING (baffling, puzzling) that many mathematicians of his day rejected it. To illustrate such strangeness, another mathematician imagined a hotel with infinitely many rooms. Even when the hotel is full, a new guest can still be given a room: every guest simply moves up one room, freeing room 1. To fit infinitely many new guests at once, every guest instead moves from room n to room 2n, emptying all the odd-numbered rooms. The idea is dizzying, and yet it is perfectly LOGICAL.

Begin with 1 and 1, then keep adding the last two numbers together: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21. This is the famous sequence named after FIBONACCI, an Italian mathematician who introduced it to Europe in 1202. It appears with startling frequency in the natural world, in the arrangement of sunflower seeds, the scales of pine cones, and the curve of nautilus shells.

Divide any Fibonacci number by the one before it and the result creeps ever closer to a special value: roughly 1.618, known as THE GOLDEN RATIO, or PHI. The golden ratio also obeys a startling IDENTITY: squaring it gives exactly the same result as adding one, so PHI squared equals PHI plus 1. Artists and architects have long claimed this proportion is unusually ELEGANT (pleasing, beautiful) to the human eye. Whether that is genuinely true or merely a persistent legend is still DEBATED, but the mathematics itself is undeniably real.

Mathematics still contains questions nobody can answer. In the year 2000, THE CLAY INSTITUTE announced seven of the hardest, called the Millennium Prize Problems, and offered a BOUNTY (reward, payment) of one million dollars for the solution to each. Only one has ever been solved.

The most celebrated of the unsolved seven is THE RIEMANN HYPOTHESIS, a deep and ELUSIVE claim about how the prime numbers are distributed. If it were proved, it would transform our understanding of number theory. Meanwhile, the one problem that has been cracked, THE POINCARE CONJECTURE, was solved by the Russian mathematician GRIGORI PERELMAN, who then astonished the world by refusing both the prize money and the medal, saying his proof was reward enough.

What actually counts as a mathematical proof? It is an argument so watertight that no exception can possibly exist. This is why disproving something can be far easier than proving it: to demolish a claim, you need only A COUNTEREXAMPLE, a single case where the claim fails. Just 1 counterexample is enough to destroy any rule, however many examples support it.

A famous warning comes from the expression n squared + n + 41, which obligingly produces a PRIME for every value of n from 0 all the way to 39. It looks like an unbreakable rule. Yet at n = 40 it collapses, and that single failure is enough. One elegant technique is proof by CONTRADICTION. You assume the opposite of what you want to prove, show it leads to nonsense, and conclude the original must be true. Mathematics also delights in A PARADOX, a statement that seems ABSURD (impossible, nonsensical) yet follows from perfectly sound reasoning. Consider the sentence 'This statement is false.' If it is true, it must be false; if false, it must be true. Such riddles are not idle games; they have driven some of the deepest discoveries in logic.
